paragraphs: Sometimes a man finally finds some real work to do. He will not need a new suit. His old one is good enough, even after a long time in the attic. Old shoes will help a hero for longer than his servant, if a hero ever has a servant. And bare feet are older than shoes, so he can use them too. Only people who go to fine parties and to parliament need new coats. They change coats as often as they change themselves. But if my jacket, trousers, hat and shoes are good enough to pray to God in, they are good enough. An old coat is never really finished. We can still give it to a poor boy. He can give it to a poorer boy, or maybe a richer one, because he needs less. I say this: be careful of any plan that needs new clothes, and not a new person inside them. If there is no new man, how can the new clothes fit? If you have a plan, try it in your old clothes. People do not want things to work with. They want something to do, or better, something to be. Perhaps we should never buy a new suit, even if the old one is torn. First we must act or try something. Then we will feel like new men in the old suit. Keeping it will feel like putting new wine in old bottles. Like birds that lose their old feathers, we must have an important moment of change. The loon, a water bird, goes alone to quiet lakes for this time. In the same way, the snake leaves its old skin, and the caterpillar its coat. They do it by growing from inside. Clothes are only our outside skin. If we do not change inside, we will look false. In the end, we will judge ourselves badly, and other people will too.

We put on one piece of clothing after another, as if we grew from the outside, like some plants. Our thin, pretty outside clothes are like a false skin. They are not part of our life, and we can take them off without danger. Our thick clothes are like the inner layer of a tree. But our shirts are like the true bark of a tree. Take off the bark all around, and the tree dies, and the man too. I believe all peoples wear something like a shirt at some times. A man should wear clothes so simple that he can find his body in the dark. He should live in a small, ready way. Then, if an enemy takes the town, he can walk out with empty hands and without fear, like the old philosopher. One thick coat is usually as good as three thin ones. Cheap clothes are easy to buy. A thick coat costs five dollars and lasts five years. Thick trousers cost two dollars. Leather boots cost a dollar and a half. A summer hat costs a quarter of a dollar, and a winter cap sixty-two and a half cents. You can make a better cap at home for very little. So who is too poor? He can wear such clothes, paid with his own work, and wise men will respect him.
